classification.difficultyReason: Determine an unknown triple intersection from overlapping totals, then interpret exclusive and complementary regions.

content.prompt:
Seventy-five students all own a dog, a cat or a bird. They were asked which pets they own. The replies gave the following information:
37 own a bird, 33 own a cat, 40 own a dog, 16 own both a cat and a bird, 11 own both a dog and a cat, 12 own both a bird and a dog.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Draw a Venn diagram representing this information.

answer.short: Bird only: 13; cat only: 10; dog only: 21; bird and cat only: 12; bird and dog only: 8; cat and dog only: 7; all three: 4; none: 0.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the number who own all three pets. The pair-only regions contain $16-x$, $12-x$ and $11-x$ students. The single-pet regions contain $9+x$, $6+x$ and $17+x$ students.
$$\begin{align*}(9+x)+(6+x)+(17+x)+(16-x)+(12-x)+(11-x)+x&=75\\71+x&=75\\x&=4\end{align*}$$
Substitution gives the region counts shown. Every student owns at least one of these pets, so the outside region is 0.

spec.sourceRegion: Challenge exercise 1(a); answer diagram on teacher PDF page 33
spec.description: Completed unshaded three-set Venn diagram. B denotes bird owners, C cat owners and D dog owners.
spec.mathematics: B only 13; C only 10; D only 21; BC only 12; BD only 8; CD only 7; BCD 4; outside 0. Region counts total 75.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; no diagram or counts supplied in the student prompt.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many students own a bird, a dog and a cat?

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the number who own all three pets. Adding the seven separate Venn regions gives:
$$\begin{align*}71+x&=75\\x&=4\end{align*}$$
Therefore, 4 students own all three pets.

children.label: c
children.prompt: A student is chosen at random and asked which pets they own. What is the probability that they own:

children.label: i
children.prompt: a cat and a dog only?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}n(\text{cat and dog only})&=11-4\\n(\text{cat and dog only})&=7\\P(\text{cat and dog only})&=\frac{7}{75}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: a bird and a dog only?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}n(\text{bird and dog only})&=12-4\\n(\text{bird and dog only})&=8\\P(\text{bird and dog only})&=\frac{8}{75}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: a bird, a dog and a cat?

answer.worked:
There are 4 students in the triple intersection out of 75 equally likely students.
$$P(\text{all three})=\frac{4}{75}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: a bird but not a cat?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}n(\text{bird but not cat})&=37-16\\n(\text{bird but not cat})&=21\\P(\text{bird but not cat})&=\frac{21}{75}\\P(\text{bird but not cat})&=\frac{7}{25}\end{align*}$$

children.label: v
children.prompt: a dog but not a bird?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}n(\text{dog but not bird})&=40-12\\n(\text{dog but not bird})&=28\\P(\text{dog but not bird})&=\frac{28}{75}\end{align*}$$
